REVIEW:
# Review: Order Online, Pick Up in Store

This is a strong memo. It corrects an inflated headline figure and shows the work, and it ties funding to evidence. I checked every calculation. The arithmetic is right, but some figures don't reconcile, and a few gaps could weaken the argument with the COO.

## Calculations check out

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| $54.8M headline | 46 × $96 × 365 × 34 = $54,802,560 | ✓ |
| Delivery: +$2.44 | 9% × $96 = $8.64; − $6.20 | ✓ |
| In-store: −$9.28 | 28% × $11 = $3.08; −$3.08 − $6.20 | ✓ |
| New: +$20.68 | 28% × $96 = $26.88; − $6.20 | ✓ |
| Blended ≈ $4 | 0.29(2.44) + 0.38(−9.28) + 0.33(20.68) = $4.01 | ✓ |
| ≈ $2.3M/year | $4.01 × 570,860 orders | ✓ ($2.29M) |
| Payback > 2 years at half volume | $2.6M ÷ $1.15M | ✓ (2.3 years) |
| Thanksgiving Nov 25, 2027 | Fourth Thursday | ✓ |

## Issues to fix

**1. The store counts add up to 31, not 34.** Wave 1 has 8 stores, Wave 2 has 12 and Wave 3 has 11. Also, if 11 stores need permits, then 23 don't, so Wave 2 should hold the remaining **15**, not 12. If the other 3 are the pilot stores already running, say so. As written, the COO will notice the gap.

**2. The $15.7M needs a short explanation.** I could only reconcile it as new-customer sales ($18.1M) minus lost impulse purchases ($2.4M). That's a sensible net figure, but "genuinely new sales" suggests the gross number. Add a few words, for example "net of lost impulse purchases."

**3. The $35 minimum isn't derived.** The economics differ by order type:
- New customers break even at about $22 ($6.20 ÷ 28%).
- Orders that switch from delivery break even at about $69 ($6.20 ÷ 9%).
- Orders that switch from in-store shopping lose money at any basket size.

Show how you got $35, or call it a starting point to test in Wave 1.

**4. The "33% may be new" assumption is the weak point, and the memo doesn't say so.** If the new-customer share falls below about **20%** (with the difference coming from in-store shoppers), the contribution per order turns negative. One sentence on this would show the COO that the cannibalization rate matters more than order volume, and it would tell the May gate review what to measure.

**5. Costs left out of the payback.** The two-year payback at half volume already excludes substitutions, marketing and possibly bay construction, so the real figure is longer. Also say whether the $6.20 picking cost includes the $1.10/hour clerk premium. If it doesn't, every per-order figure is overstated.

## Smaller points

- **The recommendation and the gate conflict.** The opening commits to all 34 stores by mid-October, but the May gate says "proceed only if results justify it." Consider "phased rollout toward all 34 stores, subject to a May gate review."
- **Gate data will be thin.** Wave 1 stores that open in late April will have only weeks of data by May, and early numbers may reflect launch novelty. Consider basing the gate on stores open at least 6–8 weeks.
- **Permit timing.** Permits are filed in January, but arrival is counted "from February." Pick one.
- **"Substituted for 7% of products"** is unclear. Use "7% of ordered items were substituted." Also estimate the cost (refunds, lost repeat orders), since the memo excludes it from profit.
- **Permit spending.** The permit filings happen before the gate, so say whether they come out of the first tranche.
- **Formatting.** There is an empty `##` heading at the end of the document. Delete it.

## Overall

The main argument holds: about $4 per order and roughly $2.3M a year at best, not $54.8M. Fix the store count and explain the $15.7M and $35 figures before it goes to the COO. Adding the 20% break-even point would make the case for gating funding much stronger.
